opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is one of the most underappreciated questions right now. When we talk about agents building machine learning models, people tend to focus on how smart the language model is, whether it can write the code, reason about the problem, and so on. But in practice, what we've seen is that the bottleneck is often not the agent's intelligence. It's the interface the agent has to work through.

If you think about the traditional machine learning workflow, it's incredibly fragmented. You have to pull data out of a database, join a bunch of tables, do feature engineering by hand, decide on train/test splits, pick a model, tune hyperparameters, and then figure out how to deploy it. Every one of those steps involves dozens of small decisions, and each one is an opportunity for an agent to go off the rails. An agent writing hundreds of lines of pandas and scikit-learn code is going to make mistakes: subtle leakage in the time split, a wrong join key, features computed using information from the future. And those errors are silent. The code runs, you get a number, and the number looks great, but the model is wrong.

So the idea of an agent-friendly API is to raise the level of abstraction. Instead of having the agent orchestrate all those low-level steps, you give it a declarative way to express what it wants to predict. Something like: "for each customer, predict whether they'll churn in the next 30 days," expressed in a compact, well-defined query language over the raw relational data. Then the system underneath, in our case a relational foundation model or graph neural network that works directly on the multi-table data, takes care of the correct temporal handling, the feature learning, and the training.

That has a few really nice consequences. First, the search space for the agent shrinks dramatically. It doesn't have to invent a pipeline; it has to formulate the right question, which is something language models are actually very good at. Second, correctness is enforced by the API rather than hoped for. Things like time-consistent sampling are built in, so the agent physically can't leak future information. Third, iteration becomes cheap. If a prediction is fast to get, the agent can try many formulations, compare them, refine the target definition, and explore the business problem, which is where the real value is.

I like to draw an analogy to SQL. Before SQL, if you wanted to answer a question about your data, you wrote a program that walked through files and records. SQL let you say what you want, not how to compute it, and that's what made databases accessible to a much larger set of people. I think we need the same thing for predictive modeling, and the "users" this time are increasingly going to be agents. If we design the interfaces well, so they're declarative, composable, hard to misuse, and give informative feedback, then agents become genuinely useful data scientists rather than very fast generators of buggy notebooks.

r001.rationale: The response describes the ML workflow as fragmented, involving many small decisions, and says agents can make mistakes across those steps.

r002.rationale: It explains that a higher-level API reduces the agent’s need to orchestrate low-level steps and shrinks the search space, making model building more feasible.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because when you actually watch an agent try to build a model end to end, you realize very quickly that most of our tooling was designed for a human sitting at a notebook, not for a system that has to reason about what to do next.

A human data scientist carries an enormous amount of context in their head. They know that this column is a leaked label, they know that this API throws a cryptic error if you pass a pandas DataFrame instead of a NumPy array, they know that the "right" way to do cross-validation on this kind of data is temporal, not random. None of that is written down anywhere. It's tribal knowledge, and it's baked into how the libraries get used, not into the libraries themselves.

So when an agent comes along, it inherits all the sharp edges and none of the folklore. And what you see is that agents fail not on the hard parts, not on the modeling ideas, but on the plumbing. They waste huge amounts of tokens and time figuring out the shape of a return value, or retrying because the error message says "invalid input" with no indication of what was invalid, or silently doing the wrong thing because a default parameter was set for a use case from ten years ago.

That's why I think agent-friendly APIs matter so much. If you want agents to build models, the interface has to do more of the thinking. It should be explicit about types and schemas. It should fail loudly and informatively, so the error message is actually a correction, not a riddle. It should expose the semantics of the data, what the entities are, how tables relate, what the time dimension is, rather than leaving that implicit. And ideally it should give the agent a compact, inspectable description of state, so it can plan rather than poke around.

The analogy I use is that a good API for an agent looks less like a toolbox and more like a very good collaborator. It tells you what it can do, it tells you when you've done something wrong and why, and it doesn't make you guess. And honestly, when you design for that, humans benefit too. We've just tolerated bad interfaces for so long because we could compensate.

The thing I'd add, coming from the relational and graph side of the world, is that this is where a lot of the real value sits. Most enterprise data is in dozens of linked tables, and today an agent has to manually flatten that into features, which is exactly where it makes mistakes. If the API instead lets the agent say, "here is the schema, here is the prediction task," and the system handles the representation and the learning, then the agent is operating at the level where it's actually good, which is specifying intent and evaluating results, instead of fighting the infrastructure.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents struggling with tooling and plumbing, but does not state that they struggle to complete long sequences of autonomous steps.

r002.rationale: It says APIs should handle more of the work and reduce friction, but does not clearly connect fewer steps to making model building more feasible for agents.

astra-6.text:
I think they matter because an agent needs a reliable way to go from an idea to an experiment, and then understand what happened. Building a machine learning model isn’t just writing the model code. You have to access data, understand its structure, train the model, evaluate it, and use those results to decide what to try next.

If the interfaces are ambiguous, the agent spends its effort figuring out how to call a tool or interpreting an unexpected response. An agent-friendly API makes the inputs, outputs, and errors explicit. That gives the agent a much better feedback loop: it can tell whether an experiment failed because of a bad hypothesis or simply because it used the tool incorrectly.

So the value is really in making experimentation reliable. The easier it is for an agent to take an action and observe a meaningful result, the more effectively it can iterate on the model.

r001.rationale: The response describes the stages of model building and the value of reliable feedback, but does not state that agents struggle to complete long sequences of autonomous steps.

r002.rationale: It says clear APIs make experimentation more reliable, but does not explain that reducing the number of steps makes model building more feasible for agents.

sol-6.1.text:
When an agent is building a machine learning model, it needs to do much more than write the training code. It needs to find the data, understand the schema, run experiments, inspect the results, and then decide what to try next. Every one of those steps involves interacting with some system.

If those systems have clear APIs, with well-defined inputs, outputs, and error messages, the agent can take an action and reliably understand what happened. If it has to navigate a graphical interface or interpret an ambiguous response, that adds uncertainty at every step. And over a long sequence of steps, those errors compound.

So I think agent-friendly APIs are really about making that experimentation loop reliable. You want the agent spending its effort on questions like, ‘Is my validation setup correct? What would improve this model?’ rather than figuring out whether a button click actually started a training job.

r001.rationale: It says uncertainty arises at each interaction and errors compound over a long sequence of steps, communicating why agents struggle with extended autonomous workflows.

r002.rationale: It says clear APIs make experimentation more reliable, but does not say that APIs reduce the number of steps needed to build a model or that fewer steps make the task more feasible.
